\chapter{The Table Is Set}
\label{ch:gu-table-is-set}
\hlchaptermodality{31}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can hear and say five everyday Gujarati food words, and read and write one of them.}

Five food words enter meaning-first by ear, one lesson each; an oral checkpoint scores listening and speaking apart, rice reaches the page with signs taught before chapter 8, and an R1 return carries the chapter-16 table back at its fourth spacing window.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[bhāt]{\gu{ભાત} — hear rice}

\label{lesson:GU-C27-hear-bhaat}



\begin{quote}
Say the Gujarati word for the flatbread you met in the water-and-tea chapter. Now listen twice: \textbf{bhāt}. It means \textbf{rice} — cooked rice, the base of the plate, not the raw grain.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bhāt\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bhāt\textquotedblright{} twice, once slowly and once at speed
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{bhāt} mean? (\textbf{Rice.})

Source: \href{https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english-gujarati/rice}{Cambridge: rice}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dāḷ]{\gu{દાળ} — hear lentils}

\label{lesson:GU-C27-hear-daal}



\begin{quote}
Say the word for rice. Now listen twice: \textbf{dāḷ}. It means \textbf{lentils} — cooked lentils, the other half of the pair Gujaratis name in one breath as \emph{dāḷ-bhāt}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}dāḷ\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bhāt\textquotedblright{} for rice, then \textquotedblleft{}dāḷ\textquotedblright{} for lentils
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{dāḷ} mean? (\textbf{Lentils.})

Source: \href{https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english-gujarati/lentil}{Cambridge: lentils}.
\end{tcolorbox}

\section[kerī]{\gu{કેરી} — hear mango}

\label{lesson:GU-C27-hear-keri}



\begin{quote}
Say the word for oil, then the word for flatbread. Now listen twice: \textbf{kerī}. It means \textbf{mango} — the fruit of the hot months, and note it ends in \emph{-ī}, exactly like \emph{roṭlī}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kerī\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tel\textquotedblright{} for oil, then \textquotedblleft{}kerī\textquotedblright{} for mango
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{kerī} mean? (\textbf{Mango.})

Source: \href{https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english-gujarati/mango}{Cambridge: mango}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Five things on one plate, by ear}

\label{lesson:GU-C27-plate-five}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new arrives here. Say the first and the last word of the chapter before any list is read to you.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Keep two scores. \textbf{Listening} goes from sound to meaning; \textbf{speaking} goes from meaning to sound. A strong score in one cannot cover a miss in the other. The third row is not new material — it is the eight time words of the day-and-its-times chapter, returning about thirty lessons on at their third spacing window.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two of the five would a Gujarati name in one breath? (\textbf{dāḷ} and \textbf{bhāt}.)

Sources: \href{https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english-gujarati/rice}{rice}, \href{https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english-gujarati/lentil}{lentil}, \href{https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english-gujarati/vegetable}{vegetable}, and \href{https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english-gujarati/mango}{mango}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Bhāt reaches the page}

\label{lesson:GU-C27-bhaat}



\begin{quote}
Before anything is uncovered, say the Gujarati word for \textbf{rice}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Uncover \textbf{\gu{ભાત}} once. Three pieces, none new: \textbf{\gu{ભ}} from the courtesy chapter, the \textbf{\gu{ા}} stroke from the greeting, and \textbf{\gu{ત}} beside it. Name the pieces aloud in order, then read the whole word once. This is the only word of the chapter the hand is asked for; the other four stay in the ear for now, which is the gloss-first order rather than an omission.

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy, model in view}
Keep the model in view and copy \textbf{\gu{ભાત}} once. Repair one shape if it needs it; do not start a row.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many signs make \emph{bhāt}, and was any of them new today? (\textbf{Three}, and \textbf{none} was new.)

Source: \href{https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english-gujarati/rice}{Cambridge: rice}.
\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection*{Your turn — the distant band, the water, tea, milk, and bread you asked for long ago}
These three were introduced around position 100 and have not been asked for since. At this position they are more than a hundred lessons old, which is the fourth spacing window rather than the third.

\subsection*{Writing — from sound, every model covered}
Record \textbf{writing} on its own; a 5/5 in listening cannot cover a miss here.
